items.stem: Which of the following best describes "memoir"?
options: A first-person account focusing on particular memories or a period of the writer's life, with reflection
The individual circumstances – family, place, experiences – that shaped a person
An account of a person's life written by that person, usually covering a long period
A short, interesting story about a real incident
items.answer: A first-person account focusing on particular memories or a period of the writer's life, with reflection
items.markingKey: A. "memoir" is a first-person account focusing on particular memories or a period of the writer's life, with reflection.

items.stem: Explain the difference between autobiography and biography.
items.answer: A biography is written by someone else in the third person and relies on research; an autobiography is written by the subject in the first person from personal memory.
items.markingKey: A biography is written by someone else in the third person and relies on research; an autobiography is written by the subject in the first person from personal memory. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following memoir extract by a writer remembering her first day in a new country.

I was nine when we arrived in Oslo in January. I had never seen snow, and I had never been so cold that my teeth hurt.
My mother bought me a red coat from a charity shop. It was two sizes too big. 'You will grow into it,' she said, and she was right, though not in the way she meant.
That coat went everywhere with me – to my first Norwegian lesson, to my first sleepover, to the school where nobody could say my name.
I still have it. It fits now. So does the city.

Outline the conventions of the text type used here, with examples from the extract.
items.answer: It is a memoir extract. Conventions: a first-person adult narrator looking back on real events, with reflection on what they meant. In this text, for example: "It fits now. So does the city." (parallel short sentences) and the list of places the coat went, each chosen to suit the purpose and audience.
items.markingKey: It is a memoir extract. Conventions: a first-person adult narrator looking back on real events, with reflection on what they meant. In this text, for example: "It fits now. So does the city." (parallel short sentences) and the list of places the coat went, each chosen to suit the purpose and audience. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from the autobiography of a cricket coach who grew up in Colombo.

I learned to bat with a coconut-palm branch and a tennis ball wrapped in electrical tape. Our pitch was the lane behind my uncle's shop, and the stumps were a stack of bricks.
The rules were simple: hit the shop window and you were out – and you also had to explain it to my uncle.
I was eleven when I hit the window. I still remember the sound: not a crash, but a tiny, terrible click.
My uncle didn't shout. He handed me a broom and said, 'Now you learn to sweep, then you learn to aim.' I have been coaching young players with that sentence for thirty years.

Identify the type of life writing and explain two features that show this.
items.answer: It is autobiography: a first-person account of the writer's own life, told by an older narrator looking back, combining specific childhood memories with reflection on how they shaped him.
items.markingKey: It is autobiography: a first-person account of the writer's own life, told by an older narrator looking back, combining specific childhood memories with reflection on how they shaped him. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Identify whether each text is autobiography, biography or memoir: (a) "Jesse Owens was born in Alabama in 1913..." (b) "I was nine when we arrived in Oslo..." with reflection on belonging.
items.answer: (a) biography; (b) memoir.
items.markingKey: (a) biography; (b) memoir.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Autobiography is more truthful than biography."
items.answer: Each has strengths and limits: autobiography offers inner truth but may be biased; biography offers research and distance but cannot fully know the subject's feelings.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the writer lived the events; it gives direct access to feelings. Arguments against: writers may hide or flatter themselves; biographers can check sources and be more objective. Supported judgement: Each has strengths and limits: autobiography offers inner truth but may be biased; biography offers research and distance but cannot fully know the subject's feelings.

items.answer: Life writers select, shape and interpret events; memory is imperfect and biographers choose which facts to include.

items.stem:
Read the following short biography of the athlete Jesse Owens.

Jesse Owens was born in Alabama in 1913, the grandson of enslaved people. His family moved north to Ohio, where a school coach noticed how fast he ran.
In 1936 the Olympic Games were held in Berlin. Germany's Nazi government wanted the Games to show that its idea of racial superiority was true.
Owens won four gold medals – in the 100 metres, 200 metres, long jump and relay.
Yet when he returned to the United States, he still faced segregation. 'I wasn't invited to shake hands with the President,' he later said.

What features of biography or autobiography are used in this extract?
items.answer: It is a biography: third-person, chronological, factual (dates, places, medal events), with a quotation from Owens himself as evidence.
items.markingKey: It is a biography: third-person, chronological, factual (dates, places, medal events), with a quotation from Owens himself as evidence. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

My uncle didn't shout. He handed me a broom and said, 'Now you learn to sweep, then you learn to aim.' I have been coaching young players with that sentence for thirty years.

How does the writer make this childhood memory vivid and meaningful?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: Specific details – the coconut-palm bat, the taped ball, the stack of bricks – recreate the improvised street game. The humorous rule foreshadows the incident, and the unexpected sound "a tiny, terrible click" captures his dread. The uncle's calm words become a lesson, and the final reflection links the anecdote to thirty years of coaching.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Specific details – the coconut-palm bat, the taped ball, the stack of bricks – recreate the improvised street game. The humorous rule foreshadows the incident, and the unexpected sound "a tiny, terrible click" captures his dread. The uncle's calm words become a lesson, and the final reflection links the anecdote to thirty years of coaching. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.answer: perspective
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of perspective.

items.stem:
Read the following short biography of the environmental activist Wangari Maathai.

Wangari Maathai was born in 1940 in a village in central Kenya, where she fetched water from a stream lined with fig trees.
In 1971 she became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate. But she noticed that the streams of her childhood were drying up as forests were cut down.
In 1977 she founded the Green Belt Movement, paying rural women to plant trees. Together they planted tens of millions.
In 2004 she became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

How does the writer use historical or personal context in this extract?
items.answer: Historical context: Kenya in the 1970s faced deforestation and women had few opportunities; Maathai connected environmental damage with poverty and women's rights. Personal context: her childhood memory of the stream shows why she cared about trees.
items.markingKey: Historical context: Kenya in the 1970s faced deforestation and women had few opportunities; Maathai connected environmental damage with poverty and women's rights. Personal context: her childhood memory of the stream shows why she cared about trees. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Explain why understanding historical context changes how we read a life story.
items.answer: Context shows the obstacles a person faced and why their actions mattered; Owens's medals mean more when we know about Nazi propaganda and segregation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Context shows the obstacles a person faced and why their actions mattered; Owens's medals mean more when we know about Nazi propaganda and segregation. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Context is just extra information and does not affect meaning." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Context shapes meaning: the same achievement can be ordinary or extraordinary depending on the barriers of the time.
items.markingKey: Context shapes meaning: the same achievement can be ordinary or extraordinary depending on the barriers of the time. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "You cannot understand a life story without knowing its historical context." Discuss.
items.answer: Context deepens understanding significantly, though some aspects (emotions, relationships) can be appreciated without detailed historical knowledge.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: context explains obstacles and choices; readers may misjudge actions without it. Arguments against: personal feelings and universal experiences can be understood without context; texts often provide the context needed. Supported judgement: Context deepens understanding significantly, though some aspects (emotions, relationships) can be appreciated without detailed historical knowledge. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem:
Read the following diary entry by a 13-year-old on a school expedition in the Scottish Highlands.

Wednesday 14 May
Today was the WORST and maybe the BEST day of my life.
We walked 18 km in the rain. My boots filled with water like two buckets. Leo's map blew into a loch. We argued for twenty minutes about which way was north.
Then the clouds split open and there it was: the whole valley, gold and green, with a rainbow sitting on it like a crown.
Nobody said anything for ages. Even Leo stopped complaining.
Tomorrow: 22 km. Help.

Rewrite the diary entry as a short report (about 150 words) for the school newsletter about the expedition.
items.answer: Indicative content: headline; third-person or "we" voice; facts (distance, weather, location); a quotation from a student; formal or semi-formal register; no private feelings in diary style.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: headline; third-person or "we" voice; facts (distance, weather, location); a quotation from a student; formal or semi-formal register; no private feelings in diary style. Indicative content above. Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Autobiographical writing should always tell the exact truth."
items.answer: Life writing should be honest about real events, but writers inevitably shape memories; the key is emotional and factual honesty rather than perfect recall.

Arguments against: memory is imperfect, so some reconstruction is inevitable; shaping events can reveal emotional truth. Supported judgement: Life writing should be honest about real events, but writers inevitably shape memories; the key is emotional and factual honesty rather than perfect recall.

Owens won four gold medals – in the 100 metres, 200 metres, long jump and relay.
Yet when he returned to the United States, he still faced segregation. 'I wasn't invited to shake hands with the President,' he later said.

How does the biographer use context to make Owens's achievements more meaningful?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The biographer begins with his family history (grandson of enslaved people) and places the 1936 Games in their Nazi propaganda context, so his four gold medals become a challenge to racist ideas. The ironic turn "Yet ... he still faced segregation" and his own quotation show that his achievement did not free him from racism at home.

The ironic turn "Yet ... he still faced segregation" and his own quotation show that his achievement did not free him from racism at home. items.stem: "You cannot understand a life story without knowing its historical context." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Context deepens understanding significantly, though some aspects (emotions, relationships) can be appreciated without detailed historical knowledge.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: context explains obstacles and choices; readers may misjudge actions without it. items.stem:
Read the following short biography of the environmental activist Wangari Maathai.

Wangari Maathai was born in 1940 in a village in central Kenya, where she fetched water from a stream lined with fig trees.
In 1971 she became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate. But she noticed that the streams of her childhood were drying up as forests were cut down.
In 1977 she founded the Green Belt Movement, paying rural women to plant trees. Together they planted tens of millions.
In 2004 she became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

Which features of the extract show that it is a particular text type? Give examples.
items.answer: It is a biography extract. Conventions: a third-person account of a real person's life, using facts, dates, sources and quotations. In this text, for example: "the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize" (superlative / "first") and the link between the childhood stream and the later drying streams, each chosen to suit the purpose and audience.
items.markingKey: It is a biography extract. Conventions: a third-person account of a real person's life, using facts, dates, sources and quotations. In this text, for example: "the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize" (superlative / "first") and the link between the childhood stream and the later drying streams, each chosen to suit the purpose and audience. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Explain the difference between historical context and personal context.
items.answer: Historical context is the wider situation of the time (wars, laws, social attitudes); personal context is the individual's own circumstances (family, childhood, experiences).
items.markingKey: Historical context is the wider situation of the time (wars, laws, social attitudes); personal context is the individual's own circumstances (family, childhood, experiences). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following diary entry by a 13-year-old on a school expedition in the Scottish Highlands.

Wednesday 14 May
Today was the WORST and maybe the BEST day of my life.
We walked 18 km in the rain. My boots filled with water like two buckets. Leo's map blew into a loch. We argued for twenty minutes about which way was north.
Then the clouds split open and there it was: the whole valley, gold and green, with a rainbow sitting on it like a crown.
Nobody said anything for ages. Even Leo stopped complaining.
Tomorrow: 22 km. Help.

Analyse the effect of the date and first-person present reflection in the text.
items.answer: The date and first-person present reflection: they show the diary's private, immediate voice.
items.markingKey: The date and first-person present reflection: they show the diary's private, immediate voice. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.answer: Life writers select, shape and interpret events; memory is imperfect and biographers choose which facts to include.

items.answer: Context shapes meaning: the same achievement can be ordinary or extraordinary depending on the barriers of the time.

items.stem:
Read the following memoir extract by a writer remembering her first day in a new country.

I was nine when we arrived in Oslo in January. I had never seen snow, and I had never been so cold that my teeth hurt.
My mother bought me a red coat from a charity shop. It was two sizes too big. 'You will grow into it,' she said, and she was right, though not in the way she meant.
That coat went everywhere with me – to my first Norwegian lesson, to my first sleepover, to the school where nobody could say my name.
I still have it. It fits now. So does the city.

How does the writer use the red coat to show her changing sense of belonging?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The coat is a symbol: "two sizes too big" suggests the new country first felt too large and unfamiliar. Her mother's words gain a double meaning ("not in the way she meant") as the narrator grows into a new identity. The list of places shows gradual adaptation, and the final parallel sentences "It fits now. So does the city." link coat and country, showing she now belongs.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Autobiographical writing should always tell the exact truth."
items.answer: Life writing should be honest about real events, but writers inevitably shape memories; the key is emotional and factual honesty rather than perfect recall.
